extracted.intended_audience: European traders, colonial administrators, plantation investors and planners involved in West African trade and development (late-19th century context)
extracted.subtask_short: developing West Africa trade and plantations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for establishing, transporting, and commercializing natural-resource extraction, riverine/coastal trade, and plantations on the West African coast; discusses transport, soils, crops, labour, and investment strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectation of African riches
rubrics_metrics.description: Africa does not possess ready-made riches to the extent it is in many quarters regarded as possessing; it requires hard work to get resources out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat West Africa as containing valuable resources 'in the structure' rather than obvious surface treasures; plan for sustained, difficult extraction rather than quick pickings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel qualities for successful trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful work on the West Coast requires 'men endowed with great luck, pluck, patience, and tact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit leaders and managers able to tolerate hardship, fever risk, slow returns, and difficult relations with natives and middlemen; personal resilience and diplomacy are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold assessment of natural resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide consideration of natural resources into (1) the means of working these resources as they at present stand; (2) the possibility of increasing them by introducing new materials of trade-value (tea, coffee, cocoa, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both current extractive infrastructure and the feasibility of plantation/introduction schemes before investing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate maritime liner service and routes
rubrics_metrics.description: The West Coast has regular steam-liner services (English lines: Elder Dempster, British African, Royal African; Woermann; French Chargeurs Reunis and Fraissinet; Portuguese Empreza Nacional) with varying frequencies and terminus patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether regular weekly/fortnightly/monthly steam services call at your port of interest; know which lines serve which ports and their freighting habits when planning exports/imports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess landing hazards (surf and bars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Landing difficulties (Gold Coast surf, Lagos bar, South-west Coast 'Calemma') make getting cargo on board expensive and risky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey local surf, bar depth and surf-boat options; factor surf-boat cost, lifespan, and limitations into logistics and infrastructure cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer waterways and small river steamers over long railways
rubrics_metrics.description: Interior waterways are virtually roads; small suitably-built river steamers are likely more repaying than lines of railway in many districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise use and development of navigable rivers (Cross River, Volta, Ancobra) and investment in river steamers where possible, especially for early-stage penetration of the interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Railways only where necessary into the interior
rubrics_metrics.description: Railways are essential in certain points (e.g., Lagos, Gold Coast) but are often not the best first investment for West Africa generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If building railways, route them inland toward productive districts rather than hugging the coast; avoid railways that merely connect coastal points unless justified by traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics for landing railway plant through surf
rubrics_metrics.description: Landing railway material through the surf is a great difficulty and enormously expensive unless mitigated (e.g., piers or small bar boats).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for specialized landing craft or alternative landing sites/upstream assembly to avoid prohibitive surf-landing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for native middlemen and transport costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Native middlemen exact high tolls (example: 75% in some cases); transporting goods inland (e.g., to Coomassie) may involve high carrier costs that make white traders uncompetitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate carrier fees, time, and losses; consider how existing native trade networks and tariffs will affect the margin for imported goods in interior markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roads may not substitute for river/steam transport for trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide engineered roads may be less useful than shaded bush paths for native carriers; roads may have military value but not necessarily improve bulk transport by carriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overvalue road construction as a means to reduce carrier costs; appraise whether roads will actually lower transport costs or only serve administrative/military purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reckless heavy expenditure opening country prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: Reckless expenditure in attempts to open up the country hampers future development (mortgages too heavy; failures discourage further efforts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage investments conservatively; prioritise economically justified, low-capital-first approaches (e.g., river steamers, small pioneer expeditions) over speculative large-scale rail projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for pioneer exploration and possession before exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pioneer explorers (de Brazza, Binger, Zintgraff) are required to extend possessions to command interior trade routes; 'do your pioneer work first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support or wait for systematic exploration and territorial control to secure interior trade routes before investing heavily in infrastructure that depends on those routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil selection for plantations: plant on hard-wood forest soils
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not start a plantation on soil that is not growing hard-wood forest; sour sandy clay and mangrove-reclaimed soils are poor choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of indigenous hard-wood forest as a rough indicator of suitable plantation soil; avoid newly exposed or deforested areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deforested and harmattan-affected tracts for cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deforested areas on the Gold Coast (and harmattan/long dry season) make land useless for cultivation even if soil was once good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical land use and climatic patterns; degraded lands may require long rehabilitation or be uneconomic for plantations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer volcanic/rich soils (Cameroons, Fernando Po, Principe, San Thome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regions of richest soil are in German/French/Portuguese possessions (Cameroons, Fernando Po, Principe, San Thome) — rich volcanic earths favourable to plantations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target volcanic/river-rich districts for plantation investments where climate and water distribution are suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crop suitability: coffee, cacao, rubber preferred; tea doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: Coffee and cacao are likely profitable; tea 'barely worth trying' except possibly in Cameroons/Congo Francais; Para rubber does well but is slow to mature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select crops suited to local climate and labour skills; plant long-term crops like rubber early due to multi-year maturation; be cautious about introducing tea without skilled labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perennial crop timescale consideration (e.g., Para rubber)
rubrics_metrics.description: Para rubber 'must be left at least three or four years before it is tapped at all' — not a quick cropper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multi-year production lag in financial plans; ensure capital and management can sustain plantations through immature years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour skill and temperament limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Great hindrance to plantation enterprise is the difficulty of getting neat-handed, skilful native labour; Africans may be unsuitable for delicate tasks (e.g., tea rolling) and require close supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for intensive training, supervision, and possibly imported skilled labour for delicate processing; account for high labor-management costs and potential low productivity for certain crops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health and mortality constrain labour deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: The West African climate cannot be relied on for white labour due to malaria, malarial typhoid, and blackwater; plantation work must be organised with local labour solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not plan operations that depend on sustained white labour presence; design labour systems around local ethnic labour sources with awareness of health risks and seasonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and use local labour pools selectively (Kruman, Accra, Sierra Leonian)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kruman, the Accra, and the Sierra Leonian are current practical labour solutions: Kruman good for ship-and-beach work, Accra/Sierra Leonian useful as artisans/clerks/overseers but limited for plantation manual work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit labour according to ethnic/regional specialisms; use Kruman for coastal work, Accra/Sierra Leoneans for skilled roles and supervision, and recognise limitations for bulk plantation tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use economic cost comparisons: waterways vs railways (Elliot's figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: a steamer on Victoria Nyanza could be placed at cost ~12,677 pounds and convey cargo far cheaper than an 18-mile railway (~53,000 pounds), making river transport much cheaper per ton-mile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform capital and operating cost comparisons when choosing between river steamers and railways; waterways often give far better short-term economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government role and subsidy in pioneer work
rubrics_metrics.description: Pioneer work must be undertaken, or subsidised by the Government as in the French possessions; 'the West Coast does not offer those inducements to the ordinary traveller' so state assistance may be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for or seek government subsidies/assistance for initial exploration, botanical stations, and infrastructure to reduce private pioneer risk.
